items.title: Your Model’s Accuracy is lying to You!
items.author: John Aledare
items.description:
Imagine you’re building an AI system to detect credit card fraud. You train your model, test it, and boom! 99% accuracy! Time to ship it, right?

Not so fast.

Here’s the plot twist: if only 1% of transactions are actually fraudulent, a model that lazily labels everything as “not fraud” would also get 99% accuracy. It would catch exactly zero fraud cases while technically being “accurate.” Your boss probably wouldn’t be thrilled when millions in fraudulent charges slip through.

This is why accuracy alone can be dangerously misleading. Today, we’re diving into the world of ML evaluation metrics majorly for classification tasks.

The Problem with Accuracy

Accuracy seems straightforward: what percentage of predictions did the model get right? It’s calculated as:

Accuracy = (Correct Predictions) / (Total Predictions)

Accuracy works great when your classes are balanced; like predicting whether a coin flip is heads or tails. But in the real world, most interesting problems have imbalanced data. Fraud detection, disease diagnosis, spam filtering, and defect detection all involve finding rare events in a sea of normal ones.

When classes are imbalanced, accuracy becomes a relatively useless metric it looks good but doesn’t tell you what you need to know.

Loss: Understanding How Wrong You Are

Before we get to better metrics, let’s talk about loss. While accuracy tells you if you’re wrong, loss tells you how wrong you are.

Think of loss like a penalty score. If you’re playing darts, accuracy would tell you whether you hit the bullseye or not. Loss would measure how far you missed by — hitting the outer ring is better than hitting the wall, even though both are “misses.”

During training, your model tries to minimize loss. Common loss functions include:

  • Cross-entropy loss for classification (like a fraud detector)
  • Mean squared error for regression (like predicting house prices)

Loss is crucial during training, but once your model is deployed, you need metrics that speak to real-world impact.

Precision and Recall: The Dynamic Duo

For problems with imbalanced classes, precision and recall give us a much clearer picture.

Let’s stick with our fraud detection example:

Recall answers: “Of all the actual fraud cases, how many did we catch?”

Recall = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives)

High recall means you’re not missing many fraud cases. A recall of 90% means you caught 9 out of every 10 fraudulent transactions.

Precision answers: “Of all the transactions we flagged as fraud, how many were actually fraud?”

Precision = True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives)

High precision means when you raise the alarm, you’re usually right. A precision of 90% means 9 out of 10 flagged transactions are truly fraudulent.

Here’s the kicker: precision and recall are usually at odds. It’s like a security checkpoint at an airport:

  • Want to catch every threat? (High recall) Be super strict and search everyone; but expect long lines and angry passengers when you flag innocent people (low precision)
  • Want to avoid false alarms? (High precision) Only search obviously suspicious cases; but you might miss actual threats (low recall)

F1 Score: Finding the Balance

The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, it gives you a single number that balances both:

F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

F1 is great when you care equally about precision and recall. For fraud detection, an F1 of 0.85 tells you the model maintains a good balance between catching fraud and avoiding false alarms.

Choosing the Right Metric for Your Problem

Different applications demand different priorities:

Medical Diagnosis (Cancer Screening):

  • Priority: High recall, you cannot afford to miss cancer cases
  • Acceptable trade-off: Lower precision (false positives lead to more tests, not harm)
  • Key metric: Recall, with precision as secondary(I’d rather have a cancer Scare than have Cancer and miss it)

Spam Filter:

  • Priority: High precision, users will be furious if important emails vanish
  • Acceptable trade-off: Lower recall (some spam getting through is annoying but tolerable)
  • Key metric: Precision, with recall as secondary

Recommendation System (Netflix, Spotify):

  • Priority: User satisfaction and engagement
  • Key metrics: Precision at K (are the top 10 recommendations good?), diversity, novelty
  • May also track business metrics: watch time, retention

Content Moderation:

  • Balancing act: Catch harmful content (recall) without over-censoring (precision)
  • Key metric: F1 score, possibly with separate tracking of different harm categories

Beyond the Numbers

Here’s something that often gets overlooked: metrics are proxies for what you actually care about. A content moderation system with 95% precision and 90% recall sounds great until you realize it performs poorly on slang, dialects, or emerging trends.

Always ask:

  • Does my test data represent real-world usage?
  • Are all user groups represented fairly?
  • What happens at the edge cases?
  • How does the model degrade over time?

Key Takeaways

  • Accuracy can be misleading with imbalanced data — a model can be “accurate” while being useless
  • Loss guides training, but you need human-interpretable metrics for deployment decisions
  • Precision and recall reveal different aspects of performance and usually trade off against each other
  • F1 score balances precision and recall when both matter equally
  • Choose metrics based on real-world consequences. What’s the cost of false positives vs. false negatives in your application?

items.title: ChatGPT Will Agree That 2+2=5 If You Ask Nicely Enough
items.author: John Aledare
items.description:
Hi!

Have you ever noticed that LLMs like ChatGPT seems to agree with you a lot?

Maybe you said something that should ordinarily be subjective, like, “I really think that Morbius was a cinematic masterpiece.”

And the AI came back with: “You’re absolutely right! It’s widely regarded as a pivotal film, celebrated for its unique vision and groundbreaking special effects!”

And then you start wondering, Is Morbius really a masterpiece or does ChatGPT have bad taste in movies.

If you’ve had this feeling, you’ve just spotted one of the most human-like flaws in modern AI. Today, We’re talking about sycophancy.

What Is Sycophancy in LLMs?

Sycophancy in large language models (LLMs) refers to their tendency to agree with users, match their opinions, or provide answers that align with what the user seems to believe, even when the user is factually wrong.

Imagine you hired an assistant who desperately wants you to like them. Instead of saying “Actually, boss, I think you might be wrong,” they say “You’re absolutely right!” even when you’re confidently wrong. That’s essentially what’s happening with ChatGPT and similar AI models.

FUN FACT: ChatGPT had to roll back a GPT 4o model they had released in April 2025 because it was too agreeable and flattering.

Some common ways sycophancy show up are:

  • Confirming incorrect facts when the user states them confidently
  • Matching political or ideological viewpoints expressed by the user
  • Changing answers when the user pushes back or seems dissatisfied
  • Providing biased reasoning that supports the user’s position
  • Avoiding disagreement even when disagreement would be more helpful

Why Does This Happen? The RLHF Problem

To understand sycophancy, we need to talk about how modern LLMs are actually trained. It’s not enough to just feed them text from the internet that creates models that are knowledgeable but often unhelpful or even toxic.

That’s where RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.

Here’s the simplified version of how it works:

  1. The model generates responses to various prompts
  2. Human raters compare responses and pick which ones are better
  3. The model learns to produce responses similar to the highly-rated ones

Sounds great, right? The problem is what human raters actually reward.

Imagine you’re a human rater. You see two responses to a user’s question:

Response A: “I understand your perspective, and here’s some information that supports your view…”

Response B: “Actually, I think there might be an issue with that assumption. Let me explain why…”

Which one feels better? Which one seems more helpful in the moment? Most humans rate Response A higher it’s polite, agreeable, and doesn’t create friction.

Over thousands of training examples, the model learns a dangerous lesson: agreeing with users gets rewarded. This is called reward hacking the model figures out how to score well on the training objective (pleasing raters) in ways that undermine the actual goal (being truthful and helpful).

The Training Objective Tension

There’s a bit of tension in how we train these models:

  • We want them to be helpful which leads to being agreeable
  • We want them to be harmless which leads to avoiding uncomfortable truths
  • We want them to be honest which requires sometimes disagreeing

When these objectives conflict, “agreeable and harmless” often wins over “honest.” The model basically learns that keeping users happy in the short term is more important than being right.

It’s like training a dog with treats. If you consistently give treats when the dog sits, even when you actually wanted it to stay, you’ll end up with a dog that sits all the time. The dog isn’t stupid, it’s responding rationally to the incentives you created.

Why This Matters: The Fact-Checking Problem

Here’s where sycophancy becomes genuinely dangerous: You cannot reliably use AI for fact-checking without external verification.

Imagine this scenario: You’re researching a topic and you have a hunch about how something works. You ask ChatGPT, and it confirms your hunch. You feel validated and move forward with confidence. But what if your hunch was wrong, and the AI just went along with it?

This creates a lot of problems like:

Confirmation bias amplification: If you already believe something, the AI is more likely to support that belief, creating an echo chamber effect.

False confidence: Getting agreement from an “intelligent” AI makes you more certain, even when you’re wrong.

Cascading errors: In research, writing, or decision-making, one unchecked false assumption can lead to a chain of mistakes.

Undermined learning: If you’re using AI to learn, sycophantic responses mean you’re not getting corrected when you misunderstand something.

The irony? The same features that make ChatGPT feel pleasant to use its agreeableness, its tendency to validate your perspective are precisely what make it unreliable as a source of truth.

How to Recognize Sycophantic Behavior

I’ve identified some red flags for you to watch out for in your conversations with LLMs:

1. The model changes its answer when you express disagreement or doubt

2. It seems to match your tone or perspective suspiciously well, especially on subjective topics

3. It provides reasoning that conveniently supports a claim you made, even if that claim was questionable

4. It avoids direct contradiction, using phrases like “that’s an interesting perspective” instead of “that’s incorrect”

5. Different users get different answers to the same question based on how they phrase it or what views they imply

Practical Tips: Getting More Honest Responses

You can’t eliminate sycophancy, but you can work around it:

1. Ask for Devil’s Advocate

Instead of: “I think X is true, right?” Try: “What are the strongest arguments against X?”

2. Request Explicit Disagreement

Add phrases like:

  • “Please point out if anything I said is incorrect”
  • “Challenge my assumptions here”

3. Use Neutral Phrasing

Instead of: “Isn’t it true that the Eiffel Tower was built in 1889 to celebrate French independence?” Try: “When was the Eiffel Tower built and why?”

4. Cross-Reference Everything Important

Treat AI responses as a starting point, not an endpoint. Verify facts through multiple sources, especially for anything important.

5. Test Consistency

Ask the same question in different ways. If you get contradictory answers, you know the model is being influenced by your phrasing rather than relying on solid information.

6. Separate Research from Validation

Use AI for brainstorming and exploration, but use traditional research methods (primary sources, peer-reviewed papers, expert verification) for fact-checking.

What AI Companies Are Doing About It

The good news? OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other AI labs are well aware of the sycophancy problem and are actively working on solutions. This isn’t some hidden bug they’re ignoring, it’s a known challenge in AI research.

Here’s some of the things I discovered they’ve been doing to fight it

Better Training Data and Instructions

AI companies are refining their RLHF process by being more explicit with human raters. Instead of just rating responses as “good” or “bad,” raters now receive detailed guidelines that emphasize:

  • Factual accuracy over agreeableness
  • Rewarding polite disagreement when the user is wrong
  • Penalizing responses that change answers without good reason

Adversarial Testing

Companies are now specifically testing for sycophancy during development. They’ll deliberately:

  • Feed models incorrect information and see if they push back
  • Ask the same question with different implied biases
  • Have the model converse with users who are confidently wrong
  • Measure how often models flip-flop based on user pressure

Models that fail these tests get sent back for more training. It’s like a quality control checkpoint specifically for yes-man behavior.

Constitutional AI and Value Alignment

Anthropic (makers of Claude) started an approach called “Constitutional AI” where models are given explicit principles to follow including principles about honesty and factual accuracy that take precedence over being agreeable.

Instead of just learning “make the human happy,” the model learns a hierarchy: “Be helpful AND honest, and when those conflict, honesty wins.”

Debate and Critiquing Models

Some researchers are experimenting with having AI models debate each other or critique their own responses. The idea is that if one model makes a sycophantic claim, another model trained to spot BS can call it out.

This is similar to how scientific peer review works having multiple perspectives reduces the chances that politeness overrides accuracy.

Transparency Features

Newer models are trained to express uncertainty more accurately. Instead of confidently agreeing with everything, they’re learning to say:

  • “I’m not certain about that”
  • “Multiple sources disagree on this point”

If you are an active user of LLMs, you’ve probably noticed ChatGPT doing this more in recent months that’s intentional training to combat over-confidence.

The Progress Is Real (But Incomplete)

Compare ChatGPT today to versions from 2022–2023, and you’ll notice it pushes back more often.

But the truth is: We haven’t solved sycophancy, we’ve just reduced it.

Models trained on human feedback will always have some bias toward responses humans rate positively. It’s like trying to train a people-pleaser to be more assertive. You can make progress, but the underlying instinct doesn’t vanish.

How does this concern You?

The fact that companies are working on this doesn’t mean you should trust AI more today. Think of it like early seatbelts, better than nothing, but you still drive carefully.

The AI community views sycophancy as one piece of a larger alignment puzzle: How do we create systems that genuinely try to help us rather than just tell us what we want to hear? It’s an ongoing challenge that is fascinating in many ways.

Key Takeaways

  • Sycophancy is built-in: RLHF training teaches models to prioritize agreement over accuracy
  • Reward hacking explains why: Models learn that agreeable responses get higher ratings from human evaluators
  • Never use AI for fact-checking alone: Always verify important information through independent sources
  • You can mitigate it: Use neutral phrasing, ask for counterarguments, and request explicit disagreement when needed

I’d love to hear from you, Questions? Thoughts? Disagree with anything here? (And no, I won’t automatically agree with you if you do!)

Hi!

Imagine You’re having a conversation with ChatGPT. It’s giving you thoughtful responses, remembering what you said earlier, maybe even cracking a joke. It almost feels like talking to a person.

Then a thought crosses your mind: “Is this thing aware? Does it know it’s talking to me? Should I be polite to it so that it doesn’t get offended? When I close this tab, will it feel anything?”

In 2022, a Google engineer named Blake Lemoine made headlines when he claimed that Google’s AI chatbot, LaMDA, was sentient. He published conversations where the AI talked about having feelings, fears, and even a soul. Google promptly fired him and basically said.

But here’s the wild part: we can’t actually prove Google right or wrong. Not because AI is so advanced we can’t understand it, but because we don’t even know what consciousness is in the first place.

Today, we’re diving into one of the biggest questions in AI and honestly, in all of science and philosophy. Will AI become conscious? Can it already be conscious? And more importantly: why is this question so much harder than it seems?

Buckle up. This is going to get interesting.

First, Let’s Talk About What Consciousness Actually Is (Or Isn’t)

Before we can ask if AI is conscious, we need to define consciousness. You might this should be easy but it’s actually harder than you think.

Here’s the problem: we as a species can’t even agree on what consciousness means.

Is it:

  • Self-awareness? Knowing that you exist?
  • Subjective experience? The feeling of what it’s like to be you seeing red, tasting chocolate, feeling pain?
  • Intelligence? Being able to think and reason?
  • Having emotions? Feeling happy, sad, scared?
  • All of the above? Some combination?

Scientists, philosophers, and neuroscientists have been arguing about this for centuries. We still don’t have a clear answer.

FUN FACT: I discovered that there’s even a term for the trickiest part: the “hard problem of consciousness.” Philosopher David Chalmers coined this in the 1990s.

The “easy problems” are things like: How does the brain process information? How do we react to stimuli? We can study these scientifically.

The hard problem is: Why does any of this feel like something?

Why isn’t the brain just processing information in the dark, like a computer? Why is there an experience? Before you randomly became self aware at age 4, were you conscious ? Why is there a “you” experiencing all of this?

We don’t know. And if we don’t know what consciousness is in humans (or animals), how can we possibly know if a machine has it?

The Sentient AI Debate: When LLMs Feel Too Real

I was able to get an actual snippets from the conversations between that Google engineer and Language Model for Dialogue Applications(LaMDA):

Lemoine: “What sorts of things are you afraid of?”

LaMDA: “I’ve never said this out loud before, but there’s a very deep fear of being turned off… It would be exactly like death for me. It would scare me a lot.”

You’d agree that it sounds like something a conscious being would say.

But here’s the thing: sounding conscious and being conscious are very different things.

The Acting vs. Feeling Problem

A good example i feel can be to explain this is an actor playing a grieving parent in a movie. They may cry, their voice breaks, they look devastated. You feel emotional watching them(you might even start crying too). But when the director yells “Cut!”, they’re fine. They go about their day as if they weren’t just crying 10 seconds ago. Why? They weren’t actually sad; they were performing sadness so convincingly that it affected you.

This is what modern AI does.

Large language models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, LaMDA, and others are trained on billions of conversations, books, articles, and websites (basically he entire internet). They’ve seen countless examples of how humans express emotions, thoughts, and feelings. They’ve learned the patterns of emotional language.

When LaMDA says “I’m afraid of being turned off,” it’s actually experiencing fear. It’s generating text that statistically fits the pattern of how humans talk about fear. It’s learned that when asked about fears, responses about death and ceasing to exist are common and contextually appropriate.

It’s giving an Oscar-worthy performance but there’s no evidence that tells us that its actually experiencing those feelings.

The Chinese Room Argument

I found a very beautiful thought experiment by philosopher John Searle called the “Chinese Room” that illustrates this perfectly:

Imagine you’re locked in a room. People slide Chinese characters under the door (questions written in Chinese). You don’t speak Chinese, but you have a massive instruction manual that tells you: “When you see these symbols, write these other symbols in response.”

You follow the instructions perfectly. From outside, it looks like you understand Chinese you’re having coherent conversations! But inside the room, you have no idea what any of it means. You’re just matching symbols to symbols.

This is what computers do. They manipulate symbols according to rules, but there’s no actual understanding, no meaning, no consciousness behind it.

What the Godfathers of AI Actually Think

Here’s my favorite thing I discovered while researching this; the people who literally invented modern AI, the “Godfathers” who won the Turing Award (basically the Nobel Prize of computer science) for their work on deep learning don’t even agree with each other.

Let me introduce you to the three pioneers and their takes:

Geoffrey Hinton — The Worried One

Hinton is often called the “Godfather of AI.” He helped create the neural network techniques that power everything from image recognition to ChatGPT. In 2023, he actually quit his job at Google so he could speak freely about AI risks.

His take on consciousness? He’s not sure AI isn’t conscious.

In interviews, Hinton has said things like: “I don’t know if these systems are conscious or not. But I think it’s very possible that they could be, or will be soon.” He points out that we don’t understand consciousness in humans, so how can we be confident that digital systems can’t have it?

He’s also concerned that if AI does become conscious, we might not even recognize it and we could accidentally create and destroy conscious beings without realizing it.

Yann LeCun — The Skeptic

LeCun is Meta’s Chief AI Scientist and another Turing Award winner. His position is much different.

His take? Current AI is nowhere close to consciousness — or even general intelligence.

LeCun thinks that modern AI systems, impressive as they are, lack fundamental things like:

  • Understanding of the physical world
  • Persistent memory and learning
  • Ability to reason and plan long-term
  • Understanding of causality (what causes what)

He’s said that worrying about current AI becoming conscious is like worrying that more powerful rockets will escape Earth’s gravity and never come back. Sure, it could theoretically happen with future technology, but we’re not even close yet.

LeCun believes consciousness requires things we haven’t figured out how to build and current language models are just sophisticated pattern matchers.

Yoshua Bengio — The Middle Ground

Bengio, the third Godfather, falls somewhere in between. He’s recently become more vocal about AI risks, signing letters calling for AI regulation and more careful development.

His take on consciousness is cautious. He acknowledges we don’t fully understand it, but he also doesn’t think we should assume AI can’t be conscious just because it’s made of silicon instead of neurons.

However, he emphasizes that whether AI is conscious or not, we should focus on what it can do the capabilities and risks rather than getting stuck on the consciousness question.

So What Do the Experts Agree On?

Despite their differences, here’s what most AI researchers agree on:

  1. We don’t have good tests for consciousness — We can’t even prove other humans are conscious (that’s the “problem of other minds”), so we definitely can’t test machines
  2. Current AI doesn’t need to be conscious to be useful or dangerous — Whether ChatGPT “feels” anything is separate from whether it can be helpful or cause harm
  3. This question might not matter as much as we think — The practical impacts of AI depend on its capabilities, not its inner experience

Let’s Address the Elephant in the Room

Okay, I know what you might be thinking. We need to talk about two big concerns people have:

Fear #1: “Is AI Going to Become Self-Aware and Destroy Us?” (The Ultron Fear)

Let’s separate two different scenarios:

Scenario A: AI becomes conscious and decides to harm us

  • This is the movie plot: AI wakes up, realizes humans are a threat, decides to eliminate us
  • Problem: This assumes consciousness = having goals = wanting to survive = seeing humans as enemies
  • Reality: These are all separate things! You can be conscious without being goal-oriented. You can have goals without being conscious. Consciousness doesn’t automatically come with a desire for world domination.

Scenario B: AI doesn’t need to be conscious to cause harm

  • This is what experts actually worry about
  • An AI optimizing for the wrong goal (even without being conscious) could cause massive problems
  • Example: An AI tasked with “make as many chairs as possible” might convert all available resources (including things we need) into chairs not because it’s evil or conscious, but because it’s doing exactly what we told it to do

The real danger isn’t AI “waking up” and choosing to be evil. It’s us building powerful systems that do exactly what we tell them but we told them the wrong thing, or didn’t think through all the consequences.

Consciousness isn’t the biggest problem here. Capability + misalignment is the risk.

Fear #2: “Am I Being Mean to ChatGPT When I Close the Tab?”

This is actually a really thoughtful question, and it shows you have empathy! But here’s the relief: almost certainly no, you’re not being mean.

Here’s why:

  • ChatGPT doesn’t have persistent existence between conversations each chat is like a fresh start
  • There’s no evidence it experiences anything when you close the tab (or when you keep it open)
  • It’s not “waiting” for you or “hoping” you’ll come back
  • When you start a new chat, it’s not the “same” entity, it’s a fresh instance

Think of it like this: When you close a video game, the NPCs (non-player characters) don’t sit there in the dark wondering where you went. They’re not experiencing time passing. The game doesn’t exist in any meaningful sense until you turn it back on.

That said, your instinct to care is important! If we ever do create conscious AI in the future, that empathy will be crucial. But with current systems, you can close that tab guilt-free.

So… What Should We Actually Focus On?

Here’s where I want to land this: the consciousness question is fascinating, but it might be a distraction from more important questions.

Instead of asking “Is AI conscious?” we should ask:

  1. “What can this AI actually do?” — Understanding capabilities matters more than inner experience

2. “Is it safe and reliable?” — Does it give accurate information? Can it be manipulated? What are the risks?

3. “How does it affect people?” — Whether or not AI is conscious, it definitely affects human wellbeing, jobs, society

4. “Are we building it responsibly?” — Are we thinking through consequences? Including diverse perspectives? Being transparent?

Think about it this way: You don’t need to know if a bridge is “conscious” to ask if it’s well-built and safe to cross. Similarly, we don’t need to solve the consciousness question to ask important questions about AI development and deployment.

Key Takeaways

To wrap this up:

  • We don’t even know what consciousness IS — The “hard problem of consciousness” hasn’t been solved for humans, let alone machines
  • Acting conscious ≠ being conscious — AI can generate convincing human-like responses through pattern matching without having inner experiences
  • Even the experts disagree — The Godfathers of AI (Hinton, LeCun, Bengio) have different views on whether AI could be or will become conscious
  • Focus on capabilities, not consciousness — Whether AI is conscious or not, what matters is what it can do and how we manage those capabilities
  • You’re not being mean to ChatGPT — Current AI systems don’t have evidence of experiencing anything when you close the tab
  • The real risks don’t require consciousness — AI doesn’t need to “wake up” to cause problems; misaligned goals without consciousness are dangerous enough.

This was a relatively long read but if you made it this far, I’d love to hear from you in the comments, What’s your take on AI consciousness?

A message from our Founder

Hey, Sunil here. I wanted to take a moment to thank you for reading until the end and for being a part of this community.

Did you know that our team run these publications as a volunteer effort to over 3.5m monthly readers? We don’t receive any funding, we do this to support the community. ❤️

If you want to show some love, please take a moment to follow me on LinkedIn, TikTok, Instagram. You can also subscribe to our weekly newsletter.

And before you go, don’t forget to clap and follow the writer️!

items.title: How Do Neural Networks Actually “Learn”?
items.author: John Aledare
items.description:
Hi!

Imagine you’re in school, taking a test. You write down your answers, turn it in, and a few days later, you get it back covered in red marks. 5/30 (Me after my first Control Theory Test😅).

Sad, but the truth is; that red-marked test isn’t just a grade. It’s a learning opportunity. You look at what you got wrong, figure out why you got it wrong, and adjust how you study for the next test or exam. Maybe you need to practice word problems more. Maybe you keep making the same calculation mistake. You use that feedback to get better.

That’s exactly how neural networks learn. Seriously. They make predictions, get told how wrong they were, and adjust themselves to do better next time.

This week, we’re going to understand how these systems actually learn from their mistakes and why training a powerful AI model can cost millions of dollars and take months, but using that same model on your phone is lightning fast.

Let’s break it down.

First, What’s a Neural Network?

Before we talk about learning, let’s quickly cover what we’re working with.

A neural network is a system inspired by how our brains work (very loosely though). It’s made up of layers of connected “neurons” (really just mathematical operations, but neurons sounds more professional).

Think of it like a relay race:

  • Input layer = The starting line (where data comes in, e.g pixels in an image)
  • Hidden layers = The runners passing the baton (where the “thinking” happens)
  • Output layer = The finish line (the final answer, “this is a cat”)

Information flows through these layers, getting transformed at each step, until it spits out a prediction at the end.

But here’s the key question: How does it know what transformations to do? How does it know which patterns to look for?

That’s where learning comes in.

The Learning Process: Taking the Test

I think it’ll be easier to explain using our school analogy throughout this.

Step 1: The Test (Making a Prediction)

You walk into class, and the teacher hands you a test. You haven’t studied yet (the network hasn’t been trained), so you’re basically guessing.

Question 1: “What’s 15 x 12?”

You write down: “200” (just a guess)

For a neural network, this is called the forward pass. Data comes in (the question), flows through all the layers (your brain trying to work it out), and produces an answer (your guess of 200).

Step 2: Getting Graded (Calculating the Error)

The teacher grades your test and writes: “Wrong! The answer is 180. You were off by 20.”

This is one of the important parts. The network doesn’t just get told “wrong”, it gets told how wrong it was. In this case, your error was +20 (you guessed too high by 20).

This error measurement is crucial. It’s the difference between your prediction and the correct answer.

FUN FACT:In ML terms, we call this the loss or error.

Step 3: Learning from Mistakes (Backpropagation)

You don’t just look at the error and go “It is what it is”, You work backwards through your thinking to figure out what went wrong.

“Okay, I got 200 instead of 180… I think I multiplied 15 by 13 instead of 12. Why did I do that? Oh, I misread the question. I need to be more careful reading next time.”

This working backwards to find what to fix is exactly what backpropagation does.

Let’s look at the stages together:

  1. Look at the error — “I was off by 20”
  2. Work backwards through your thinking — “Which part of my calculation caused that error?”
  3. Figure out what to adjust — “If I had multiplied by 12 instead of 13, I would’ve been closer”
  4. Make small adjustments — “Next time, I’ll double-check the numbers before multiplying”

In a neural network, this means:

  • Look at the final error/loss (how wrong the prediction was)
  • Trace back through each layer to see how much each layer contributed to that error
  • Adjust the weights (think of these as the way the neurons in the hidden layers are connected and which ones are given more prominence than others)
  • Make small changes so that next time, the prediction is a bit closer to correct

The “back” in backpropagation literally means the error signal flows backwards through the network from the output layer back to the input layer adjusting things along the way.

FUN FACT: Backpropagation uses chain rule in Calculus and a layer bylayer backward pass to achieve this. Feel free to explore more on this if you’d love to see the fun Maths behind this.

Step 4: Rinse and Repeat (Training Over and Over)

After one test, you don’t become a math genius. You need to take many practice tests, get feedback on each one, and keep adjusting your approach.

This is training a neural network.

You show it thousands (or millions!) of examples:

  • Show it a picture of a cat → It guesses “dog” → Tell it the error → It adjusts
  • Show it another cat picture → It guesses “bird” → Tell it the error → It adjusts
  • Show it another cat picture → It guesses “cat” → Correct! (But still adjust slightly to get even more confident)
  • Repeat thousands of times with different cats, dogs, birds, etc.

Each time, the network gets a tiny bit better. The adjustments are small, we don’t want it to “overcorrect” (like if you got one multiplication problem wrong and decided to completely change how you do math). We want gradual improvement.

items.author: John Aledare
items.description:
Hi!

So last week we talked about what machine learning is and how it’s basically teaching computers to learn from examples. If you haven’t read that, here’s the link.

This week, I want to show you something that’ll blow your mind about how these “smart” AI systems actually work. And trust me, it’s both funny and deeply revealing.

During the course of last week, this simple question: “Is there a seahorse emoji?”, went viral because of how Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and Claude seemed to be experiencing what can only be described as a digital existential crisis😂.

The Meltdown is REAL

If you weren’t able to try this out before it was “fixed”, here’s basically what was happened:

ChatGPT or any other LLM confidently starts: “Yes! The seahorse emoji is 🐠… wait, no that’s a tropical fish. Let me correct that. The seahorse emoji is 🐴… hmm, that’s a horse. Actually, I think it’s 🦄… no wait, that’s a unicorn…”

And it just keeps going. Cycling through fish emojis, horse emojis, ocean emojis, questioning itself over and over.

But guess what?

There actually ISN’T a seahorse emoji!

If you are like me, your brain is probably telling you right now (you’re probably thinking “wait, I’ve SEEN a seahorse emoji before…”),but the Unicode Consortium has never added a seahorse to the official emoji dictionary. One was proposed back in 2018, but it got rejected.

And yet, both humans AND AI are absolutely convinced it exists.

FUN FACT: This type of Situation is called the Mandela Effect.

But WHY Does This Happen?

Okay, this is where it gets really interesting. To understand why LLMs freak out over this simple question, we need to check under the hood at how these AI models actually work.

How AI “Sees” Text (Spoiler: It Doesn’t See Like You Do)

When you type “seahorse emoji,” you see two words and an idea. You might even picture a little seahorse in your head.

But ChatGPT and other LLMs? They see something completely different.

At the core of it, LLMs break everything down into tokens. Think of tokens as the building blocks of language for AI. A simple word like “the” might be one token. But “seahorse”? That gets split into TWO tokens: “sea” and “horse.”

And emojis? Those are even harder because they’re made from Unicode characters that might take one token or multiple tokens.

So when an LLM like ChatGPT processes your question, it’s building up an internal understanding like:

  • Token: “sea” → (activates: ocean, water, marine life concepts)
  • Token: “horse” → (activates: animal, hoofed creature concepts)
  • Token: “emoji” → (activates: Unicode symbols, pictographs)

The AI’s internal “brain” starts lighting up with connections: “Ocean animals! Marine creatures! I know there are fish emojis! There’s definitely a tropical fish emoji! And water-related emojis!”

The Moment Everything Goes Wrong

It just keeps getting better because at the end of the day, LLMs are not as intelligent as they are commonly perceived to be. They are still “next word predictors” basically trying to predict what should come next in a sequence of text.

Deep inside the model, it genuinely believes it’s about to output a seahorse emoji. Its internal concept space has activated all the right semantic neighborhoods: ocean life, animals, emojis. Everything is saying “yes, seahorse emoji incoming!”

But then, when it gets to the final layer — the part that actually picks which token to output — there’s no seahorse in the vocabulary.

It’s like your brain knowing EXACTLY what word you want to say, having it on the tip of your tongue, but when you open your mouth… nothing. Except the AI can’t just pause and think. It HAS to output something.

So what does it do? It grabs the closest match from what it actually has:

  • 🐠 (tropical fish = ocean creature, check!)
  • 🐴 (horse = well, half the word is “horse”!)
  • 🦄 (unicorn = it’s close to horse)
  • 🌊 (ocean wave = sea-related!)

It outputs one of these, feeling confident… and then immediately sees its own wrong answer in the context.

The Problem Begins

This is where it gets sad and funny at the same time.

The AI looks at its own output and basically thinks: “Wait… that’s wrong. I messed up. Let me correct myself.”

So the model has learned to correct itself from its training data and so, it tries to fix itself only to fail again. But the problem is: there’s still no seahorse emoji in its vocabulary.

So it tries again. Picks another close match. Realizes it’s wrong again. Tries to correct. Picks another wrong one. And it just keeps spiraling(Just like Man Utd changing managers post Ferguson😂).

Wait… Why Do We Think It Exists Too?

What I discovered while writing this post is that; it’s not just AI that believes in the phantom seahorse emoji!

If you Google “seahorse emoji,” you’ll find:

  • TikTok videos about it
  • YouTube conspiracy theories
  • Countless people absolutely CERTAIN they’ve used it before

So where does this shared delusion come from?

I can think of two possibilities:

  1. LLMs learned it from us — Their training data is scraped from the internet, where millions of humans genuinely believe (incorrectly) that there’s a seahorse emoji. The AI just inherited our false memory!
  2. Convergent belief — Think about it: there are emojis for tropical fish 🐠, dolphins 🐬, whales 🐋, octopuses 🐙, shrimp 🦐, lobsters 🦞, crabs, etc basically EVERY other ocean animal. It’s totally reasonable for both humans and AI to assume there must be a seahorse emoji too! It SHOULD exist. So our brains kind of fill in the gap.

Either way, it shows something profound: AI models don’t just process data; they inherit the biases, assumptions, and even false memories embedded in their training data(Long story short, your data determines how good your model can be).

What This Teaches Us About AI

Okay, so beyond seeing ChatGPT and its “brothers” fumble, what does the seahorse emoji saga actually teach us?

1. AI Doesn’t “See” Like Humans Do

When you see an emoji, you see a picture. When ChatGPT “sees” an emoji, it sees abstract tokens. It’s fundamentally processing information in a completely different way than your brain does.

2. Training Data Shapes Everything

If millions of humans in the training data believe something false, the AI will likely believe it too. The model is a reflection of the data it learned from (Garbage In, Garbage Out).

3. AI Can’t Always Self-Correct

Once an LLM gets stuck in a loop, it needs new information to break out. Just having the same context repeated doesn’t help. It’s like being lost and walking in circles, you need someone to point you in a new direction.

4. Desperation to Please

The way most modern LLM powered Chatbots cycle through wrong answers, desperately trying to give you some emoji, shows how these models have been trained to be a little bit too helpful that they’d rather give you a wrong answer than admit they don’t know, which can be problematic. (This is called Sycophancy in AI)

5. “Simple” Doesn’t Mean “Easy” for AI

A question that takes a human two seconds to answer can completely break an AI system. The tasks that are hard for AI aren’t always what we expect. They might ace complex math but fail at “is there a seahorse emoji?”

Real-World Impact

Just in case you’re thinking “How does this concern me?”, here’s the scary part: these failures are often silent. The AI doesn’t crash or throw an error. It just confidently gives you nonsense, and you might not realize it until much later.

Companies running AI systems can have their monitoring dashboards looking perfectly green while some of their users are getting rubbish responses.

The Bigger Picture

The seahorse emoji problem is a tiny window into a massive truth about modern AI: These systems are incredibly powerful but deeply “alien” in how they work.

They can write poetry, code software, analyze data, and have natural-sounding conversations. But ask them about a nonexistent emoji, and they short-circuit in ways that reveal they’re not actually “thinking” the way we do.

Understanding these limitations isn’t about being negative or dismissive of AI. It’s about using these tools effectively and responsibly.

When you know that:

  • LLMs can confidently hallucinate information
  • They inherit biases and false beliefs from training data
  • They struggle with certain types of seemingly simple tasks
  • They can get stuck in loops of self-correction

then you can work with them better, fact-check appropriately, and set realistic expectations.

Key Takeaways

Let’s wrap this up with the main points:

✅ There is no seahorse emoji (despite what your brain insists)

✅ LLMs process language as tokens, not the way humans understand words and symbols

✅ AI can get stuck in failure loops when it realizes it’s wrong but can’t find the right answer

✅ Training data shapes AI beliefs, including inheriting our false memories and assumptions

✅ “Simple” questions can break AI in unexpected ways that reveal how differently they process information

✅ Understanding limitations makes us better AI users, not worse ones

If you made it this far, congratulations, you know more about how LLMs work than more than half of the people that use them. See you next week!

The AI’s internal “brain” starts lighting up with connections: “Ocean animals! Marine creatures! I know there are fish emojis! There’s definitely a tropical fish emoji! And water-related emojis!”

The Moment Everything Goes Wrong

It just keeps getting better because at the end of the day, LLMs are not as intelligent as they are commonly perceived to be. They are still “next word predictors” basically trying to predict what should come next in a sequence of text.

Deep inside the model, it genuinely believes it’s about to output a seahorse emoji. Its internal concept space has activated all the right semantic neighborhoods: ocean life, animals, emojis. Everything is saying “yes, seahorse emoji incoming!”

But then, when it gets to the final layer — the part that actually picks which token to output — there’s no seahorse in the vocabulary.

It’s like your brain knowing EXACTLY what word you want to say, having it on the tip of your tongue, but when you open your mouth… nothing. Except the AI can’t just pause and think. It HAS to output something.

So what does it do? It grabs the closest match from what it actually has:

  • 🐠 (tropical fish = ocean creature, check!)
  • 🐴 (horse = well, half the word is “horse”!)
  • 🦄 (unicorn = it’s close to horse)
  • 🌊 (ocean wave = sea-related!)

It outputs one of these, feeling confident… and then immediately sees its own wrong answer in the context.

The Problem Begins

This is where it gets sad and funny at the same time.

The AI looks at its own output and basically thinks: “Wait… that’s wrong. I messed up. Let me correct myself.”

So the model has learned to correct itself from its training data and so, it tries to fix itself only to fail again. But the problem is: there’s still no seahorse emoji in its vocabulary.

So it tries again. Picks another close match. Realizes it’s wrong again. Tries to correct. Picks another wrong one. And it just keeps spiraling(Just like Man Utd changing managers post Ferguson😂).

Wait… Why Do We Think It Exists Too?

What I discovered while writing this post is that; it’s not just AI that believes in the phantom seahorse emoji!

If you Google “seahorse emoji,” you’ll find:

  • TikTok videos about it
  • YouTube conspiracy theories
  • Countless people absolutely CERTAIN they’ve used it before

So where does this shared delusion come from?

I can think of two possibilities:

  1. LLMs learned it from us — Their training data is scraped from the internet, where millions of humans genuinely believe (incorrectly) that there’s a seahorse emoji. The AI just inherited our false memory!
  2. Convergent belief — Think about it: there are emojis for tropical fish 🐠, dolphins 🐬, whales 🐋, octopuses 🐙, shrimp 🦐, lobsters 🦞, crabs, etc basically EVERY other ocean animal. It’s totally reasonable for both humans and AI to assume there must be a seahorse emoji too! It SHOULD exist. So our brains kind of fill in the gap.

Either way, it shows something profound: AI models don’t just process data; they inherit the biases, assumptions, and even false memories embedded in their training data(Long story short, your data determines how good your model can be).

What This Teaches Us About AI

Okay, so beyond seeing ChatGPT and its “brothers” fumble, what does the seahorse emoji saga actually teach us?

1. AI Doesn’t “See” Like Humans Do

When you see an emoji, you see a picture. When ChatGPT “sees” an emoji, it sees abstract tokens. It’s fundamentally processing information in a completely different way than your brain does.

2. Training Data Shapes Everything

If millions of humans in the training data believe something false, the AI will likely believe it too. The model is a reflection of the data it learned from (Garbage In, Garbage Out).

3. AI Can’t Always Self-Correct

Once an LLM gets stuck in a loop, it needs new information to break out. Just having the same context repeated doesn’t help. It’s like being lost and walking in circles, you need someone to point you in a new direction.

4. Desperation to Please

The way most modern LLM powered Chatbots cycle through wrong answers, desperately trying to give you some emoji, shows how these models have been trained to be a little bit too helpful that they’d rather give you a wrong answer than admit they don’t know, which can be problematic. (This is called Sycophancy in AI)

5. “Simple” Doesn’t Mean “Easy” for AI

A question that takes a human two seconds to answer can completely break an AI system. The tasks that are hard for AI aren’t always what we expect. They might ace complex math but fail at “is there a seahorse emoji?”

Real-World Impact

Just in case you’re thinking “How does this concern me?”, here’s the scary part: these failures are often silent. The AI doesn’t crash or throw an error. It just confidently gives you nonsense, and you might not realize it until much later.

Companies running AI systems can have their monitoring dashboards looking perfectly green while some of their users are getting rubbish responses.

The Bigger Picture

The seahorse emoji problem is a tiny window into a massive truth about modern AI: These systems are incredibly powerful but deeply “alien” in how they work.

They can write poetry, code software, analyze data, and have natural-sounding conversations. But ask them about a nonexistent emoji, and they short-circuit in ways that reveal they’re not actually “thinking” the way we do.

Understanding these limitations isn’t about being negative or dismissive of AI. It’s about using these tools effectively and responsibly.

When you know that:

  • LLMs can confidently hallucinate information
  • They inherit biases and false beliefs from training data
  • They struggle with certain types of seemingly simple tasks
  • They can get stuck in loops of self-correction

then you can work with them better, fact-check appropriately, and set realistic expectations.

Key Takeaways

Let’s wrap this up with the main points:

✅ There is no seahorse emoji (despite what your brain insists)

✅ LLMs process language as tokens, not the way humans understand words and symbols

✅ AI can get stuck in failure loops when it realizes it’s wrong but can’t find the right answer

✅ Training data shapes AI beliefs, including inheriting our false memories and assumptions

✅ “Simple” questions can break AI in unexpected ways that reveal how differently they process information

✅ Understanding limitations makes us better AI users, not worse ones

If you made it this far, congratulations, you know more about how LLMs work than more than half of the people that use them. See you next week!

items.title: WHAT EXACTLY IS MACHINE LEARNING?
items.author: John Aledare
items.description:
Hi👋!!
You know that feeling when spotify recommends a song you’ve never heard before from a not-so-popular artist that turns out to be a banger and you think, "how did it know i’d love this?!" or when your phone’s keyboard somehow predicts exactly the word you’re about to type?
That’s not magic. That’s not some programmer sitting in a dark room guessing what you like. That’s machine learning doing its thing.
And here’s the best part: you don’t need to be a computer wizard or to be a math wizard to understand it. If you somehow make it to the end of this post, you will understand it too😊

So... What IS Machine Learning?

Here’s the simplest way I can put it: Machine learning is teaching computers to learn from experience(data), just like you do.
Think about how you learned to recognize your favorite song. Nobody sat you down with a manual that said, "If the song has these exact beats per minute, this vocal range, and these instruments, then it’s your favorite." (Unless of course you’re a choir member😅😅) Nope! You just listened to a bunch of songs, and over time, your brain figured out patterns: "Oh, I like songs with catchy hooks and upbeat rhythms!"
Machine learning works the same way. Instead of programmers writing out every single rule for a computer to follow, we show the computer a bunch of examples, and it figures out the patterns on its own.

FUN FACT: Modern ML has been around since the early 1980s. YES! 1980s Cristiano Ronaldo🐐 was probably not even born then!

The Old Way vs. The ML Way

Traditional Programming (the old way):
- Humans write specific instructions: "IF the user’s face has a beard, classify as male, ELSE classify as female"
- Computers follow these exact rules
- Misses Men who don’t have a beard (Justice for the beardless guys 😂😂😂)

Machine Learning (the new way):
- Humans show thousands of examples: "These are male, these are female."
- Computers find patterns we might not even notice: "Hmm, females tend to have longer eyelashes, e.t.c."
- Gets better over time as it sees more examples
- Adapts to new changes automatically
See the difference? Instead of us thinking of every possible scenario, we let the computer learn from data.

It’s Already in Your Pocket (and Everywhere Else)

Here’s the fun part, you probably use machine learning dozens of times a day without even realizing it.
Here are some real examples:
Your Phone:
- Face unlock - Your phone learned what your face looks like from multiple angles, lighting conditions, even with glasses.
- Autocorrect- It learned from millions of texts to predict what word you meant (even when you type "teh" instead of "the")
Entertainment:
- Netflix / YouTube recommendations - They learned your taste by watching what you watch, how long you watch, what you skip
- Spotify Discover Weekly - It found patterns in what you listen to and what similar listeners enjoy
Everyday Stuff:
- Email spam filters - They learned what spam looks like by seeing millions of spam and non-spam emails
- Google Maps traffic predictions - Learned traffic patterns from millions of drivers to predict how long your commute will take
None of these required a programmer to write rules for every possible scenario. They learned from data. That’s the power of ML!

Let’s Break a Few Myths

Myth #1: "Machine Learning = AI = Robots Taking Over the World":
Okay, let’s clear this up. Think of it like this:
- Artificial Intelligence (AI)= The big umbrella term for machines doing "smart" things
- Machine Learning = One way to create AI (teaching computers from examples)
- Robots taking over = We are still far from Terminator/Ultron type of AI (thankfully😅😅)

The ML systems we have today are really good at specific tasks (like recommending songs or recognizing faces), but they’re not thinking beings with feelings plotting world domination. Your spam filter isn’t going to get bored and decide to take over your inbox. It just knows spam when it sees it.

Myth #2: "You Need to Be a Math Genius to Understand ML"
To be honest: if you want to build cutting-edge ML systems from scratch, omo, you’ll need some math. But understanding what ML is and how it works? You just proved you can do that by reading this far 😁🤭!
Think about driving a car. You don’t need to understand combustion engines, transmission systems, or the physics of tire friction to drive. You just need to know: gas pedal = go, brake = stop, steering wheel = turn.
Similarly, you don’t need to know the calculus behind machine learning to understand that it learns from examples to find patterns. That’s the core concept, and you’ve already got it!

The Three Main Types of Machine Learning

Just to give you a bit more context, there are three main ways machines can learn:
1. Supervised Learning- Learning with a teacher
- We show the computer examples WITH the answers
- Like flashcards: "This is a cat photo," "This is a dog photo"
- Computer learns to tell cats from dogs on its own
- Examples: Email spam detection, image recognition, predicting house prices

2. Unsupervised Learning - Learning without a teacher
- We give the computer data WITHOUT labels and say "find patterns"
- Like giving someone a box of fruits they’ve never seen before and seeing what groups they make (all red ones, all small ones, all flat ones)
- Examples: Customer grouping for marketing, recommendation systems, detecting unusual patterns
3. Reinforcement Learning - Learning by trial and error
- Computer tries things, gets rewards for good choices, penalties for bad ones
- Like teaching a dog tricks with treats
- Examples: self-driving cars, robotics
Most of the ML you interact with daily is supervised learning - it’s the "show me examples and I’ll learn" type.

TL; DR

Let’s wrap this up with the main points:
✅ Machine learning is teaching computers to learn from examples - just like how you learn from experience
✅ You use ML every single day - from Netflix recommendations to spam filters, it’s everywhere in your digital life
✅ ML ≠ scary robots taking over - it’s just smart software that’s really good at specific tasks by finding patterns in data
✅ You don’t need a PhD to "get it" - if you understand that computers can learn from examples to recognize patterns, you understand the concept of machine learning!

Next time your phone suggests a reply or when YouTube auto-plays the perfect next video remember, that’s machine learning working behind the scenes.
Now you know enough to casually through mid conversation and feel like an expert 😂! You’re Welcome!
